**Which question I froze.** The excerpt is from *The Time Machine*. Its opening puts one claim in the middle of the room — the after-dinner argument that Time is a fourth dimension of Space and can be travelled — so I judged that. **Frozen question:** *Is Time a fourth dimension of Space, such that a machine can carry a man along it?* Range: from the argument, through the model's vanishing, to the eight-day voyage. Kind: what produces it (forward, from causes), with one backward strand — what the model's vanishing tells us.

**The explanation in parts.**
P1 Lines and planes are abstractions, yet real enough to reason with. P2 Any real body has Duration as a fourth extension. P3 Our consciousness drifts one way along that dimension, cradle to grave. P4 Time is a kind of Space; the only difference is that consciousness moves along it. P5 The barometer's line is traced along the Time-Dimension. P6 We aren't free to move up and down either — gravitation limits us — so limited freedom in Time is no objection. P7 Vivid recall is a jump back. P8 One lever sends the machine into the future, the other reverses it. P9 The model vanishes before six witnesses and a candle blows out. P10 We can't see a machine in time because its presentation is "below the threshold", diluted. P11 Stopping is dangerous: at speed one is attenuated vapour; at rest one jams atoms into whatever is there. P12 The machine returns damaged; the Traveller returns lame, filthy, greyer.

**Part by part.** (Marks are not added up.)

| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| P1 abstractions are real enough | **held** — it blocks "you can't picture it, so it isn't real"; remove it and the argument has no floor |
| P2 Duration as a fourth extension | **held** — definitional; delete it and nothing follows |
| P3 consciousness drifts one way | **held if** — held only by "why can't we move in Time?", a job P6 and P7 answer by analogy; what would settle it: a mechanism, or a case where the drift is changed |
| P4 no difference but consciousness | **loose** — "except that our consciousness moves along it" swaps for any exception; what survives is coarser: Time is ordered and measurable like a dimension |
| P5 the barometer trace | **idle** — the line lies on the paper's own surface; remove it, alone and with P3, with no loss |
| P6 gravitation and the balloon | **loose** — swap balloon for tunnel, lift or falling; what survives is only "movement in any dimension has limits", true of everything |
| P7 recall is a jump back | **loose** — the leap is a metaphor, and it pulls against P3 |
| P8 lever forward, lever reverse | **loose** — abandoned a page later: "into the future or the past — I don't for certain know which" |
| P9 the vanishing | **held** — remove it and nothing is left; staged so a trick is closed off (six witnesses, many candles, all lit, the objector's own finger on the lever) |
| P10 diluted presentation | **loose** — a catch-all with no gauge; also **borrowed** — it rests on a psychology not tested here |
| P11 the risk of stopping | **held** — the one part with a consequence stated before the event and then paid |
| P12 damage and the Traveller's state | **two routes** — the journey, or two years at the bench; the cracked ivory bar does not separate them |
| the direction the model went | **unknown** — what would settle it: a second send with a marker inside |

**Whole-explanation checks.**
- **Flip.** Both directions are covered by the same words: "Into the future or the past — I don't, for certain, know which." The flip of the demonstration itself — nothing happens on the table, and the narrator still swears there was no trickery — would be covered too.
- **Direction.** Poke the theory (drop P2, change the number of dimensions): the machine's behaviour does not move. Poke the machine (does it vanish?): the theory does not move. The two are joined by assertion, not by a test.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** "No difference... except that our consciousness moves along it" — the exception is the whole thing to be explained and does all the work. So does "a natural infirmity of the flesh, which I will explain to you in a moment."
- **Jobs.** Given by the Time Traveller. One — would it have been visible last Thursday? — is raised by the Narrator and patched on the spot. The marker test is mine.
- **Pairs that pull.** P3 (uniform drift) against P7 (jump back). P4 (no difference) against P2 (real bodies have Duration): the more exactly Time is made like Space, the less anything explains the particular tie between the machine and the direction it moves.
- **Catch-all and gauge.** P10 swallows every failure — unseen at any speed, in either direction. It comes with no gauge: no reading that would show it swallowing a job. It is also written by the objector and produced on request ("You think. *You* can explain that"), then accepted because the Psychologist is embarrassed. That is a rescue, not a part.
- **Change list.** What it leaves out: any change that would tell a time-machine from a well-staged trick. The Medical Man names the rival — a similar thing at Tübingen, "sleight-of-hand" — and nothing on the list separates them. At this level they are the same explanation of the table.
- **Provenance.** *Built:* the geometry, and P11. *Fitted:* P10, invented after the objection. *Asserted:* the voyage. The narrator's own notice — "too clever to be believed" — says plainly the evidence is testimony.
- **Fixed:** "no interruptions", "I can't argue tonight" — the owner puts them outside the test and says so. **Free and loose, and allowed to be:** the lilies of silver, the dinner-table, the Dresden-china prettiness. These are choices, not explanations, and I am not dressing them as explained.

**What would make it harder to vary.**
1. Give P10 a gauge. Put a clock, a scale or a camera in the empty place on the table. If diluted presentation is true, some reading must differ while the machine is there — and stay put when only the reading is changed.
2. Name the direction and the return before the event: send the model away signed and dated, and say when and where it comes back.

**What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. The demonstration's tightness is Wells's staging, not the world's. A false explanation can be tightly staged; a true one can pass for bad reasons.

**One next step.** Before the next demonstration, write down one reading that would come out differently if the machine were really there — and take it whether or not it favours the Time Traveller.
